sections.heading: How does Alzheimer's disease feel and progress?
sections.body: The NHS describes Alzheimer's disease as gradual, with symptoms that develop over many years and eventually become more severe. In the early stage, small memory problems are usually the first sign, such as forgetting recent conversations or events, misplacing items or struggling to think of the right word. Anxiety, mood changes or periods of confusion can appear too, and some people have trouble judging distances or get lost in familiar places. In the middle stage, memory problems get worse, and a person may find it hard to remember the names of people they know or to recognise family and friends. Disturbed sleep, delusions and changes in mood can also occur, and by this point someone usually needs support with everyday living. In the later stage, symptoms become much more severe, with difficulty eating and swallowing, trouble moving without help, weight loss, incontinence and gradual loss of speech.

sections.heading: What other types of dementia are there?
sections.body: Alzheimer's is the most common form of dementia, and other common types include vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia. When someone has more than one type it is called mixed dementia, and the most common mix is Alzheimer's disease with vascular dementia. Young-onset dementia is dementia that begins before the age of 65. Mild cognitive impairment involves minor problems with memory or thinking, and it is not a type of dementia, but a person with it is more likely to go on to develop dementia. Memory problems are not always caused by dementia, because depression, stress, medicines, and alcohol or drugs can all cause them.

sections.heading: How is Alzheimer's disease assessed?
sections.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if you are worried about your memory or think you may have dementia. At the appointment the GP will ask about your concerns and what you or your family have noticed. You will typically be asked some questions and given memory, thinking and pen-and-paper tasks. If needed, the GP can refer you to a specialist, often at a memory clinic or memory service. These teams may include neurologists, who review brain scans, and neuropsychologists, who carry out tests of memory and thinking. Blood and other standard tests may also be done to look for other possible causes. Not everyone needs a brain scan, but for many people a CT, MRI or PET scan gives useful information, and an MRI can show which parts of the brain are shrinking. There is no single simple and reliable test, so diagnosis relies on combining history, cognitive testing and sometimes scans. The Alzheimer's Society suggests it may help to bring someone along to appointments.

sections.heading: What treatments and support are available?
sections.body: The NHS says there is no cure for Alzheimer's disease, but some medicines can temporarily ease symptoms or, for some people, slow progression. Donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine can be prescribed for early to mid-stage disease, and memantine is used for moderate or severe disease. Non-drug options include cognitive stimulation therapy, which uses group activities and exercises to build memory and problem-solving skills. Cognitive rehabilitation involves a trained professional helping the person work towards a personal goal. Reminiscence and life story work draw on photos, music and keepsakes. When someone has persistent aggression or extreme distress after other coping strategies have failed, a consultant psychiatrist can prescribe an antipsychotic such as risperidone, which has serious side effects and should be used for as short a time as possible. NICE has so far not recommended the newer medicines lecanemab and donanemab for routine NHS use, saying they are not currently cost effective, so the NICE website has the current position.

sections.heading: Living with Alzheimer's disease and caring for someone
sections.body: NHS guidance encourages staying socially active, for example through dementia-friendly groups or memory cafes where people swap practical tips. A steady daily routine is recommended, and it can encourage feelings of security and worth. Memory aids around the home can help, such as pictures on cupboard doors showing what is inside, and reminder devices or appointment alerts. General health advice covers diet, exercise, sleep, and regular dental, eyesight and hearing checks. Depression is very common in dementia, and a GP can talk through talking treatments that can help. You can ask your local council for a needs assessment, and carers can ask for a carer's assessment. NHS England describes advance care planning as fundamental for everyone living with dementia, and it can include choosing someone you trust to act for you through a Lasting Power of Attorney.

sections.heading: What are the complications and the outlook?
sections.body: The outlook varies considerably from person to person. The Alzheimer's Society says the middle stage is often the longest, while the later stage is usually the shortest. In the later stage many people have trouble eating or swallowing, which can lead to choking, chest infections and other problems. Delirium is a sudden change in mental state, where the person seems not themselves, and it is different from the slow worsening of dementia. Causes of sudden confusion include a urinary tract infection, a stroke, low blood sugar and a head injury. A urinary infection in a person with dementia can cause sudden and severe confusion. The NHS says to go to A&E or call 999 if someone suddenly becomes confused, and the Alzheimer's Society advises seeking help straight away from the GP or NHS 111 if you think a person with dementia has delirium. Dementia is the biggest single risk factor for delirium, so a change in behaviour may be missed or put down to dementia.

faqs.q: Is Alzheimer's disease the same as dementia?
faqs.a: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, but it is not the only one. Other common types include vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia. Some people have more than one type, which is called mixed dementia, and the most common mix is Alzheimer's disease with vascular dementia.

faqs.q: Is there a cure for Alzheimer's disease?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure, but some medicines can temporarily ease symptoms or, for some people, slow progression. Non-drug approaches such as cognitive stimulation therapy and reminiscence work are also used. Local councils can offer a needs assessment, and carers can ask for a carer's assessment.

faqs.q: Will I need a brain scan?
faqs.a: Not everyone does, because a brain scan is not always necessary. For many people a CT, MRI or PET scan can give useful information, either to support a diagnosis of Alzheimer's or to rule out other causes. A scan can also look normal in the early stage, when changes may not yet show.

faqs.q: Why might someone with dementia suddenly become much more confused?
faqs.a: A sudden change is different from the slow worsening of dementia and may be delirium. Causes include a urinary tract infection, a stroke, low blood sugar and a head injury. The NHS says to go to A&E or call 999 for sudden confusion, and the Alzheimer's Society advises the GP or NHS 111 straight away if delirium is suspected.

faqs.q: Should I take someone with me to a memory appointment?
faqs.a: The Alzheimer's Society suggests that it may be helpful to bring someone else along. The GP will ask what you or your family have noticed, and may ask you some questions and set memory and thinking tasks. Memory problems are not always caused by dementia, so the GP may also look for other causes.
